Issued at 328 PM EST WED NOV 11 2026

The beginning of the long term period will be characterized by 
deep 500 mb troughing over the eastern CONUS; meanwhile, an 
amplified 500 mb ridge will be centered over the High Plains, with
a closed upper level low farther west off the coast of the 
Pacific Northwest. Multiple impulses embedded within the broader 
eastern CONUS troughing will continue to support a more active 
weather pattern locally. At the surface, flow around a relatively 
deep surface low to the northeast and a surface high over western 
Ontario will support northwesterly winds, a typical upslope 
pattern. 

Given this pattern, the environment will be supportive of 
scattered precipitation across the forecast area on Friday. 
Largely northerly to northwesterly flow just above the surface 
will work to advect additional moisture from the Great Lakes into 
eastern Kentucky, although there is still uncertainty regarding 
the location of the best moisture; should low level flow be closer
to northerly, the most concentrated moisture from Lake Michigan 
could end up west of the forecast area, only being pulled into 
eastern Kentucky as the system lifts northeast, with the most 
widespread moisture entering our area in a diffuse plume 
originating from Lake Huron. Meanwhile, more northwesterly flow 
could provide a more efficient and typical Lake Michigan moisture 
fetch, resulting in better moisture overall. This will have 
implications for instability locally, with deterministic soundings
across the forecast area showing a skinny but nonzero CAPE 
profile generally concentrated in the 0 to -10C layer, indicating 
Friday's activity will likely be convective in nature. Even a few 
degree shift in dewpoints (well within the margin of uncertainty 
according to the latest ensemble guidance) could alter this CAPE 
profile, which itself could influence the ceiling of shower 
intensity. Regardless, low level moisture should be adequate for 
at least some upslope precipitation, and additional shortwaves 
should provide enough lift for scattered showers. 

Unfortunately, thermodynamics are quite marginal for a rain/snow 
mix in most lower elevation locations, introducing forecast 
uncertainty regarding precipitation type. Temperatures aloft will 
be cool, with guidance indicating 850 mb temperatures will 
generally be in the range of -4C to -5C. Meanwhile, at the 
surface, REFS mean wet bulb temperatures are generally in the 
34-36F range on Friday afternoon, with deterministic soundings 
indicating rain will likely be the primary precipitation type in 
these regions. Even so, it is worth noting that these wet bulb 
temperatures are marginal for a rain/snow mix, and the 
aforementioned uncertainty regarding moisture quality will also 
inherently introduce wet bulb temperature uncertainty. Should a 
"higher" instability solution materialize, bursts of more intense 
shower activity could introduce additional dynamic cooling in the 
column, allowing for more of a localized rain/snow mix. Given the 
potential for this cooling, in addition to expected scattered 
precipitation, temperatures were nudged down on Friday, with a 
slight chance for a rain/snow mix introduced across the forecast 
area; however, this snow potential remains highly conditional, and
any breaks in clouds could allow for diurnal heating that could 
work to offset cooling, again favoring rain. Thus, expect rain to 
be the dominant precipitation type in valley locations, and even 
if snow does fall, warm ground temperatures should prevent notable
accumulations. On the highest terrain (particularly Black and 
Pine Mountains), cooler temperatures will allow for a less 
ambiguous precipitation type, with snow being favored. Again, soil
temperatures should inhibit significant accumulations, although 
measurable snow is likely at the highest elevations. 

Looking into the weekend and beyond, a quieter pattern will set 
in. Upslope precipitation could linger over southeastern Kentucky 
into Saturday as northwest flow continues; however, aloft, the 
synoptic pattern will become significantly less active. The 
initial trough will begin to shift eastward, with intense height 
rises across the forecast area on Saturday; meanwhile, the upper 
level low initially located off the Pacific Northwest coast will 
force ridging farther east into the Plains. At the surface, high 
pressure over the Midwest and the eastward translation of the New 
England low will allow winds to gradually become more northerly 
and eventually northeasterly by Sunday, marking an end to our 
upslope regime. Temperatures will still be cool, albeit with a 
warming trend next week, which should see highs rise from the 40s 
this weekend to the upper 50s by Wednesday. Nights will be the 
coolest of the season thus far, with temperatures falling into the
